questiontext.text:
Goal

Write five short functions that hand a function around as a plain value and sort a list with a key function.

How this works in Python

A Java method is not a value. Write a method's name on its own and the compiler rejects it, because a bare name is not an expression there.

String shout(String text) {
    return text.toUpperCase() + "!";
}

shout;                                     // not an expression, will not compile
Function<String, String> f = this::shout;  // a method reference, wrapped in a functional interface

Java gives you three wrappers for moving behaviour around. A functional interface such as Function or Comparator, a lambda that implements one, and a method reference such as this::shout. The method always travels inside something else.

Python has none of that machinery, because a function already is a value. A def statement binds a name to a function object in exactly the way x = 5 binds a name to an integer.

def shout(text: str) -> str:
    return text.upper() + "!"

Once that statement has run, shout is a name holding an object, and the object happens to be callable. There is no interface to declare and nothing to wrap.

Two characters decide everything.

shout        # the function itself
shout("hi")  # the string 'HI!', which is what the function produced

Confusing those two is the first mistake a Java developer makes here, because in Java the parentheses are the only way to mention a method at all. Type them where a function belongs and you hand over the result rather than the function.

A result is usually not callable, so nothing complains at the point of the mistake. The failure arrives later, when something finally tries to call what you handed over, and it reads 'str' object is not callable.

A name holding a function behaves like any other name. Bind it to a second name, put it in a list, pass it to something, hand it back out.

same = shout
same("valve open")    # 'VALVE OPEN!'

Passing one needs no special grammar at the call site and no wrapper around the function.

from collections.abc import Callable


def apply_twice(transform: Callable[[str], str], text: str) -> str:
    return transform(transform(text))

Read Callable[[str], str] as "takes one string and hands back a string". The inner brackets hold the parameter types and the type after the comma is the return type. Import Callable from collections.abc, never from typing, which has held a deprecated copy since Python 3.9.

Returning a function needs no grammar either. A function hands back another function the way it hands back a number.

def pick_transform(loud: bool) -> Callable[[str], str]:
    return shout if loud else quiet

Neither shout nor quiet runs on that line. The caller receives one of the two function objects and decides for itself when to call it.

Sorting is where you meet all of this on an ordinary working day. Java asks the element to be Comparable, or asks you for a Comparator, which is one more functional interface to build.

words.sort(Comparator.comparingInt(String::length));

Python asks for one key function instead. sorted(items, key=f) calls f once per element and sorts on whatever comes back, so you describe the element and let Python do the comparing.

sorted(words, key=len)

len is a built-in function, and there it travels as a value with no parentheses after it. Write key=len() instead and Python calls len with no arguments on the spot, which fails before the sort has begun.

Python's sort is stable, which means two elements the key rates equal keep their original order. The test data holds two words of five letters and two of six, so you can watch that happen.

Methods are values too. str.strip is the function behind " x ".strip(), and it answers String::strip with nothing wrapped around it.

Your task

Write five short functions. Not one of them needs more than a single line of body.

  • shout(text) returns the text in upper case with ! on the end.
  • quiet(text) returns the text in lower case with . on the end.
  • apply_twice(transform, text) runs transform on text, runs it again on that result, and returns the second result.
  • pick_transform(loud) hands back the shout function when loud is true and the quiet function otherwise. It returns the function itself, never the result of calling it.
  • by_length(words) returns a new list of the words, shortest first, from one call to sorted with a key=.

The tests print the caller's list afterwards. It must come back untouched.

You pass when the printed output matches the expected text character for character.

Rules
  • Hand a function over by its name alone. The moment you type parentheses after it, you are passing its result instead.
  • Write no lambda here. Every function you need already has a name, and passing named functions around is the whole of this tier.
  • Sort with one call to sorted and one key=. No loop inside by_length, no comparison function, and no list.sort() on the caller's list.
  • Annotate every signature. A parameter holding a function takes Callable[[str], str], imported from collections.abc and never from typing.
Before you click Check

Write down what you expect each test to print. Then run it. A surprise means your model of Python is wrong, and that is the part worth learning.

AI protocol

No AI. Type every character yourself. This tier builds the muscle, and a tool that types it for you skips the exercise.

testcode.text: print(shout("all clear")) print(shout.__name__, type(shout).__name__, callable(shout)) same = shout print(same("valve open"), same is shout)

expected.text: ALL CLEAR! shout function True VALVE OPEN! True

testcode.text: print(apply_twice(shout, "pump")) print(apply_twice(quiet, "PUMP")) print(apply_twice(str.strip, " relay ") + "|") try: print(apply_twice(shout("pump"), "relay")) except TypeError as exc: print(exc)

expected.text: PUMP!! pump.. relay| 'str' object is not callable

testcode.text: transform = pick_transform(True) print(transform.__name__, transform is shout) print(transform("relay")) print(pick_transform(False)("RELAY")) readings = ["relay", "pump", "burner", "valve", "gasket"] print(by_length(readings)) print(readings) print(apply_twice.__annotations__["transform"])

expected.text: shout True RELAY! relay. ['pump', 'relay', 'valve', 'burner', 'gasket'] ['relay', 'pump', 'burner', 'valve', 'gasket'] collections.abc.Callable[[str], str]

import inspect import re
whole = "".join(inspect.getsource(f) for f in (shout, quiet, apply_twice, pick_transform, by_length)) assert "lambda" not in whole, "rule broken: every function you need already has a name" assert not re.search(r"\.sort\(", whole), "rule broken: leave the caller's list alone" assert "cmp_to_key" not in whole, "rule broken: hand over a key function, not a comparison" picker = inspect.getsource(pick_transform) assert "shout(" not in picker and "quiet(" not in picker, "rule broken: return the function, not its result" sorter = inspect.getsource(by_length) assert "key=" in sorter, "rule broken: sort with one key= and no loop" assert not re.search(r"\bfor\b", sorter), "rule broken: sort with one key= and no loop" assert "typing" not in repr(apply_twice.__annotations__["transform"]), "rule broken: import Callable from collections.abc" for fn in (shout, quiet, apply_twice, pick_transform, by_length): assert "return" in fn.__annotations__, "rule broken: annotate every return"
print(apply_twice(pick_transform(False), "Valve")) print(by_length([])) print(by_length(["bb", "a"])) print(callable(pick_transform(True)), callable(pick_transform(True)("x")))

questiontext.text:
Goal

Write six handler functions, a dict that dispatches to them, and three functions that run a command and rank faults.

How this works in Python

A Java method is not a value. To pass behaviour around you wrap it in something. You write a functional interface, or a method reference, or a Strategy class.

To dispatch on a string you write a switch. The alternative is a Map<String, Handler>, which costs you an interface, a class per handler and a static block to fill the map.

switch (op) {
    case "add" -> a + b;
    case "sub" -> a - b;
    ...
}

In Python a function is a value. def add(a: float, b: float) -> float binds the name add to a function object, exactly as x = 5 binds a name to an integer. Write add with no parentheses and you have the function itself. Write add(2, 3) and you have called it.

So a dispatch table is a plain dict whose values are functions.

OPS = {"add": add, "sub": subtract}
handler = OPS["add"]
result = handler(2, 3)

The lookup is the branch. A switch becomes a hash table rather than a chain of if statements. There is no interface to declare, and no class to write.

The table's own type is dict[str, Callable[[float, float], float]], where Callable comes from collections.abc and reads as "takes two floats, hands back a float".

An unknown command still needs an answer. OPS.get(op, other) from the dictionaries topic returns other when op is not a key, so the fallback is an argument rather than an else.

lambda makes a function without giving it a name. lambda a, b: a + b is a whole function. The body is one expression, there is no return keyword and no statements are allowed inside.

That limit is deliberate. A lambda that wants a second line wants a def.

Sorting works the same way. Java chains Comparator.comparing(...).thenComparing(...).reversed() and asks each element to be Comparable. Python asks you for one key function. sorted(seq, key=f) calls f once per element and sorts on whatever comes back.

Return a tuple from the key function and you get every tiebreak at once, because tuples compare left to right. The tuples topic gave you the tuple and the mutation topic gave you sorted, which returns a new list and leaves the caller's list alone.

sorted(faults, key=lambda fault: (-fault["severity"], fault["name"]))

That reads as severity descending, then name ascending. The minus sign flips one field on its own. reverse=True cannot do that, because it flips the whole tuple and reverses your tiebreak along with your main sort.

Python's sort is stable, which means two elements the key rates equal stay in their original order. Your tuple key leaves no ties here, so stability changes nothing in this exercise. It is worth knowing anyway.

max and min take the same key=. operator.itemgetter("severity") builds a key function that reads one dict key, so it says the same thing as lambda fault: fault["severity"] with less noise.

Your task

Write the switchboard.

  • Six small named functions, one per command, each taking a and b. They compute a + b, a - b, a * b, a / b, a // b and a % b. The numbers topic explains the last two.
  • OPS, a dict mapping the six names add, sub, mul, div, floordiv and mod to those six functions.
  • run(op, a, b) looks the handler up and calls it. For an unknown operation it falls back to a handler that returns the string unknown operation 'sqrt'. Here sqrt is whatever the caller asked for, and the !r conversion from the f-strings topic supplies the quotes. The fallback has to read op, so build it as a lambda inside run.
  • by_severity(faults) returns a new list of the fault dicts, severity descending and name ascending, from one key= that returns a tuple.
  • worst(faults) returns the single fault dict with the highest severity, using max and operator.itemgetter.

The tests print the caller's list afterwards. It must come back untouched.

You pass when the printed output matches the expected text character for character.

Rules
  • Write no if, elif or match anywhere in the dispatch path. The lookup is the branch, and the handlers are values in a dict rather than branches in a function.
  • Sort with one key= returning a tuple. No comparison function, no functools.cmp_to_key, and no returning -1, 0 or 1.
  • Do not pass reverse=True. It reverses your tiebreak along with your sort.
  • Write no class and no interface anywhere in the answer.
  • Do not call eval(). It would pass the tests, and in a safety-critical codebase it is a firing offence.
  • Leave the caller's list alone. list.sort() is banned here.
  • Annotate every signature, the six handlers included, and give OPS its Callable type as well. A table of functions should say which functions.
Before you click Check

Write down what you expect each test to print. Then run it. A surprise means your model of Python is wrong, and that is the part worth learning.

AI protocol

AI for explanation only. Ask it what an error means or why one form is more idiomatic. Do not let it write your answer.

questiontext.text:
Goal

Write a counter factory and a checker factory so every function they hand back closes over its own private value.

How this works in Python

Java lets a lambda read a local variable only when that variable is effectively final. Try to change one and the compiler stops you.

int count = 0;
Runnable r = () -> count++;   // does not compile

Java therefore captures a value, so you have never met the bug in this exercise. The usual workaround is a one-element array, because the array reference stays final while its contents do not.

int[] box = {0};
Runnable r = () -> box[0]++;   // compiles

Neither restriction exists in Python. You may write a def inside another def, and Java has no form for that. The inner function is built again every time the outer one runs.

Python captures the variable, not the value. A function defined inside another function keeps a live link to the enclosing function's locals. That link is called a closure, and the storage it points at is called a cell.

Read tick.__closure__ and you get a tuple of cells. Read cell.cell_contents and you get whatever the variable holds right now.

Python resolves a name by looking in four places in order. Local, then Enclosing, then Global, then Built-in. That order is called the LEGB rule.

Reading an enclosing variable needs nothing special. Rebinding one does. Assign to a name anywhere in a function and Python marks that name local for the whole function, so this fails.

def make_counter() -> Callable[[], int]:
    count = 0
    def tick() -> int:
        count += 1     # UnboundLocalError
        return count
    return tick

count += 1 is a read and then a write. The write makes count local, the read then finds a local with no value yet, and you get UnboundLocalError. The keyword nonlocal is the fix. It tells Python that this name belongs to the enclosing function, so leave it there.

def tick() -> int:
    nonlocal count
    count += 1
    return count

That gives you private per-call state with no class and no field. Each call to make_counter runs the body again, makes a fresh count and returns a function closed over that one. Two counters never touch each other.

Now the trap. Build functions in a loop and every one of them closes over the same loop variable. The loop reuses that variable rather than making a new one per pass.

When the loop finishes, the variable holds the last value, and every function you built sees it. No warning, and no error.

for limit in limits:
    checkers.append(lambda reading: reading > limit)

The repair is a factory function, which is a function whose whole job is to build and return another function. Call it with the value and the call gets its own local, so each returned closure gets its own cell.

A factory's return type is itself a function type, so make_counter returns Callable[[], int], where the empty brackets mean it takes no arguments at all.

Your task

unbound_demo and broken_checkers already sit in the answer box. Leave both alone, because the tests put the error and the wrong answers on screen before the fix goes on screen.

Write three functions.

  • make_counter() returns a function of no arguments. Each call to that function adds one to a count private to this closure and returns the new total. The first call returns 1.
  • make_checker(limit) returns a function that takes reading and returns reading > limit.
  • fixed_checkers(limits) returns a list of checkers, one per limit, built through make_checker.

The second test prints [30, 30, 30] from the broken checkers and True for the shared cell. The third test prints [10, 20, 30] and False. Those two lines are the whole lesson.

You pass when the printed output matches the expected text character for character.

Rules
  • Write no global and no class. The state lives in the enclosing function, and nonlocal is the tool this exercise exists to teach.
  • Do not smuggle the count in a one-element list. That is the Java workaround for a rule Python does not have.
  • Do not fix the lambdas with the i=i default-argument trick. The defaults topic told you when a default is evaluated, and this is not what defaults are for. Write a real factory function.
  • Leave broken_checkers and unbound_demo untouched. If the three broken checkers agree with each other, you have found the trap rather than fixed it.
  • Annotate every signature you write, the inner functions included. A factory returns Callable[[int], bool], and writing that down is half of what makes a closure readable to the next person.
Before you click Check

Write down what you expect each test to print. Then run it. A surprise means your model of Python is wrong, and that is the part worth learning.

AI protocol

AI allowed, on three conditions. Write your plan before you open it. Read every suggestion and reject the ones you did not plan. Type accepted code out yourself rather than pressing Tab.
